title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Sharp design wins the field test. Supply control and cash discipline decide who profits at sign-off.
epigraph.author: Industrial Underwriting Rule

web_blocks.html: AXISCADES sells through two main B2B and B2G paths [1]. It wins long-term factory slots with global plane and chip makers [1]. It also bids on Indian defense tenders under DAP 2020 [1]. Zero sales come from retail shops or local dealers [2]. All revenue comes directly from DRDO labs, BEL, HAL, and global OEMs [2].

web_blocks.caption: AXISCADES Go-To-Market, Delivery Footprint & Working Capital Mechanics
web_blocks.takeaway: Defense electronics carry multi-year qualification cycles and milestone-linked billing that elongate debtor days, whereas commercial aerospace and precision manufacturing operate on predictable 60-day invoice schedules.
rows: DAP 2020 Make-II, IDDM tenders, single-source subsystem wins
Milestone-linked: 15% advance, 70% dispatch, 15% final site acceptance.
Multi-year Master Service Agreements & build-to-spec awards
Monthly milestone or deliverable sign-off; 60–90 day collection.
AS9100 plant audits, First Article Inspection (FAI)
Batch shipment invoicing on 45–60 day credit terms.
Integrated 200-acre defense manufacturing, testing & MRO campus

web_blocks.html: Winning defense orders under DAP 2020 takes deep cash patience [3]. A private supplier must fund test gear upfront and send units to Pokhran (+50°C) and Ladakh (-30°C) [4]. Units must also pass strict interference tests and L1 price bids before billing starts [4]. Mistral also relies on imported defense FPGAs, GaN chips, and fast converters [5]. Those parts take 36 to 52 weeks to arrive [5]. That explains why raw stock sat at 121 inventory days in FY26 [6].

Even after shipment to a prime like BEL, cash waits for final system sign-off [7]. If another vendor delays a mast or power unit, Air Force checks pause and AXISCADES invoices sit unpaid [8]. Debtor days jumped from 80 days in FY23 to 89 in FY24, 107 in FY25, and 130 in FY26 [9]. The ₹100 waterfall table below traces how that delay hit FY26 cash [10].

web_blocks.caption: AXISCADES: Worked ₹100 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall (Audited FY26 Consolidated)

web_blocks.html: That ₹100 flow shows the gap between profit and cash [11]. Strong defense work lifted EBITDA margin to 15.36% and net profit to ₹6.21 per ₹100 sold [12]. Yet higher receivables and stock took ₹73 Cr in cash [13]. Operating cash flow fell to -₹1 Cr (-₹0.09 per ₹100), and plant spend led to -₹135 Cr Free Cash Flow [13].

web_blocks.mechanism: Rolta chased large Indian defense C4ISR and map orders. Accounting EBITDA margins looked high above 35%, yet unpaid bills stretched past 180–240 days. Cash flow stayed deeply negative, forcing heavy bond borrowing until defaults wiped out the firm.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: From FY13 to FY18, Rolta's receivables jumped from ₹1,120 Cr to >₹2,800 Cr and gross debt passed ₹5,300 Cr. Operating cash flow collapsed and shareholders lost over 98% of their wealth.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Rolta warns against trusting defense margins alone when debtor days pass 130 and CFO hovers near zero. Incoming Akkodis cash will help buffer AXISCADES, yet cutting debtor days remains critical.

web_blocks.html: Comparing old aero staffing against defense hardware shows why working capital swelled [7, 9]. In commercial aviation work for Airbus, monthly engineering timesheets settled quickly in 45 to 60 days [4]. In domestic defense electronics, components sit in raw stock for months before line builds begin [5, 6]. After delivery to BEL or DRDO labs, final sign-off bills often wait another three to four months [8, 9]. That shift doubled net working capital from 37 days in FY24 to 75 days in FY26 [9]. To bridge that gap, AXISCADES stretched vendor payables to 220 days and tapped bank credit lines [11]. Once Akkodis funds close, internal cash can replace bank loans while receivables run through normal military sign-offs [10].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: How Akkodis Cash Fixes Working Capital
paragraphs: Look at why the Akkodis deal ties directly to this cash table. Carrying ₹388 Cr of debt with -₹1 Cr operating cash flow while spending ₹134 Cr on plants leaves no room for error.

Freeing ~$237M (>₹2,000 Cr in phases) from Akkodis changes that math. AXISCADES can pay off loans, fund defense stock from its own cash, and skip costly NCD debt. Even then, debtor days must fall under 95 days.

book_paragraphs: If you sit down with an industrial controller who has spent twenty years financing defense contractors, they will tell you that income statements are polite suggestions, while working capital schedules are the law. And when you and I trace how an order moves from a military tender in New Delhi through AXISCADES' factory floor in Bengaluru and finally lands as cash in the bank, we quickly uncover why this business is so demanding.

Unlike a consumer software firm that swipes a credit card and receives cash forty-eight hours later, AXISCADES sells exclusively to massive institutions: Airbus in Toulouse, Bharat Electronics in Bengaluru, and India's Defence Research and Development Organisation. Under India's Defence Acquisition Procedure, winning a contract is an endurance marathon. A company often spends two years engineering a prototype at its own expense, trucking radar processors to the fifty-degree heat of the Thar Desert and the sub-zero ridges of Ladakh for user trials. Only after passing every test and winning the commercial bid does production begin.

Once production starts, the supply chain clock ticks loudly against the balance sheet. Military-grade semiconductors—radiation-tolerant FPGAs and specialized radio-frequency chips—cannot be bought off the shelf; they carry forty-to-fifty-week supplier lead times. AXISCADES has to tie up cash in raw material inventories months before assembly begins, pushing inventory days to 121 days in fiscal 2026. Worse still, when a radar processor ships to a defense public sector prime, final payment often waits until the prime integrates the entire radar mast and secures final military acceptance. Consequently, AXISCADES' debtor days climbed relentlessly from 80 days in FY23 to 130 days in FY26.

Look at the arithmetic of our worked ₹100 revenue waterfall for fiscal 2026. Out of every ₹100 of sales, AXISCADES generated a respectable ₹15.36 in operating EBITDA and reported ₹6.21 in bottom-line net profit. Yet working capital expansion swallowed ₹73 crores of cash during the year, dragging operating cash flow down to negative one crore rupees. After spending heavily on machinery and capital work-in-progress, free cash flow printed a deficit of ₹135 crores. That is why the Rolta India failure base rate sits as a permanent warning on our desk: rapid defense revenue growth without cash collection is a perilous illusion. Fortunately, the $237 million Akkodis divestment proceeds give AXISCADES the liquidity cushion to retire debt and weather these long collection cycles—provided management tightens receivable discipline as scale builds.

Every investor in Indian defense electronics must respect the cash cycle calendar. Unlike software services that collect monthly wire transfers, military hardware ties up rupee cash at two chokepoints: imported chip prepayments and post-delivery lab sign-offs. Managing that spread without piling on debt is half the battle.

Unit economics for a hardware-and-systems business can be read through three questions. How much of each rupee of revenue is spent on bought-in parts, how much on engineers and factory staff, and how long does the money stay locked before it returns? For AXISCADES the first two have improved as the mix has moved toward products. The third has worsened, and it is the one that decides whether profit becomes cash.

Look at the inventory days. At 121 days in FY26, the company carries about four months of parts and work in progress. Part of that is deliberate, because radar-grade chips have long lead times and are worth stocking. Part of it is a side effect of uneven dispatches. If a large order slips by a quarter, the parts already bought simply wait.

Now add receivables of 130 days and payables of 220 days. The company paid its suppliers slowly to compensate for collecting slowly. That is a legitimate short-term tool, but it has limits. Suppliers of specialised components will not extend credit forever, and a return to normal terms would absorb cash. The gap between these two numbers is the real size of the working-capital risk.

book_callouts.quote: Profitable growth that consumes cash faster than it collects it eventually hits a financing wall.

book_subsections.title: Navigating the DAP 2020 Gauntlet & Long-Lead Silicon Supply Chains
paragraphs: Every investor tempted by Indian defense stocks ought to sit through a single Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP 2020) procurement cycle before committing capital. Unlike commercial aerospace, where an approved Master Service Agreement with Airbus generates predictable monthly invoices on 60-day payment cycles, Indian defense electronics procurement is an obstacle course of sovereign validation. Under 'Make-II' and IDDM tracks, private companies often invest two to three years building prototypes at their own expense, enduring summer desert evaluations in Pokhran at 50 degrees Celsius and winter altitude trials in Ladakh at 15,000 feet, before an L1 commercial bid is even opened.

Even after winning an order—such as Mistral's ~₹100 crore Signal and Data Processing Unit program for DRDO and Bharat Electronics' Ashwini radar—the supply chain imposes heavy capital lock-up. Military electronics rely on radiation-tolerant FPGAs, gallium-nitride RF amplifiers, and ruggedized connectors sourced from global specialty foundries with 36-to-52-week lead times. AXISCADES must pay deposits and carry 121 days of inventory before final boards are populated, environmental-stress screened, and shipped. And once shipped to a public sector prime, the final 15% to 30% milestone cash frequently remains unpaid until the prime finishes integrating the entire radar mast and completes armed-forces acceptance testing.

book_subsections.title: Deconstructing the FY26 ₹100 Waterfall & The Rolta Warning
paragraphs: Turn to our worked ₹100 revenue waterfall for fiscal 2026, because it reveals the central tension inside AXISCADES' unit economics without a single word of corporate spin. Out of every ₹100.00 of consolidated revenue (₹1,159 crores total), operating expenses consumed ₹84.64, leaving a healthy ₹15.36 in operating EBITDA (₹178 crores). After deducting ₹3.80 for depreciation, ₹2.76 for interest expense, adding ₹1.04 of other income, and paying ₹3.62 in corporate taxes, AXISCADES posted ₹6.21 in net accounting profit (₹72 crores).

Now follow what happened below the profit line. Expanding trade receivables—as debtor days stretched from 80 days in FY23 to 130 days in FY26—plus defense inventory pre-builds swallowed ₹73 crores of cash (₹6.30 per ₹100 of revenue), pulling operating cash flow down to negative ₹0.09 per ₹100 (-₹1 crore absolute). Add ₹11.56 per ₹100 of capital expenditure and CWIP investments (₹134 crores total), and Free Cash Flow closed at a deficit of -₹11.65 per ₹100 (-₹135 crores). That is why the historical collapse of Rolta India serves as our mandatory failure base rate: prestigious defense electronics contracts and high paper EBITDA become lethal if debtor days spiral out of control and debt funds unpaid invoices. Only the incoming $237 million Akkodis proceeds shield AXISCADES from this liquidity squeeze—making debtor-day compression below 95 days non-negotiable in FY27.
